0c74c8e5708fa3db: KUALA LUMPUR: China continued to stamp their dominance at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, pulling clear at the top of the medal standings at the end of today's action.
The Chinese contingent have amassed 23 gold, 10 silver and five bronze medals for an overall total of 38, cementing their position at the top of the standings.
Hosts Japan sit second with eight golds, 12 silvers and 12 bronzes (32 medals overall), while South Korea occupy third spot with five gold, three silver and 15 bronze medals (23 overall).
Central Asian contenders Kazakhstan are fourth with four golds, one silver and three bronzes.
Thailand emerged as Southeast Asia's best performer of the day, climbing into fifth place with three gold medals and one silver.
Fellow Asean nation Myanmar also made the leaderboard with one gold, one silver and one bronze.
For the Malaysian contingent, the hunt for a breakthrough gold continues after collecting two bronze medals so far.
8040f4de3a99cd9b: GERMANY'S far right and far left both made big gains in Sunday's state elections, exposing yet again the erosion of the political centre in Europe's largest economy as well as Chancellor Friedrich Merz's weakening hold on power.

The anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) confirmed its strength in the formerly communist eastern states by taking first place in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state, building on its triumph two weeks ago in Saxony-Anhalt.
The AfD also recorded its best-ever result in Berlin, where the far-left Left Party came first and looks set to replace Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) in the mayor's office.
Merz called the result in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — the worst in CDU history — "a disaster."
But he defied speculation he might step down, pledging to remain to pass a package of tax and pension reforms that he hopes will help revive Germany's sluggish economy.

For now, at least, the party has stood behind him, although the result will add to pressure within his coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD), some of whom want to water down parts of the reform agenda.
"We have to analyse, as a government, why there is this sense of uncertainty in the country," SPD co-leader Lars Klingbeil said.
A pervasive sense of economic malaise and disillusion with traditional political parties point to further turbulence ahead, with a raft of state elections in western Germany due next year.

"Germany is entering a period of political instability where viable coalitions are harder and harder to build, and that doesn't bode well for Europe when Germany is the de facto leader," said Sudha David-Wilp, a senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the United States.

The AfD wants to expel foreigners with no right to stay in Germany, restore energy ties with Russia and quit the euro, while the Left Party wants to cap rents and nationalise large parts of the Berlin housing market.
By contrast, Merz's pursuit of what he says are painful but necessary reforms has yet to yield improvements that voters can feel.
"We can see how difficult it is to win people over while in government and from the centre of society," said Stefan Evers, the CDU's lead candidate in Berlin.
Even before the election, Merz's approval ratings were at a record low and his party has trailed the AfD in national polling for months.
"People would tell us that as long as he had a say in things, we wouldn't vote for you," said one CDU election campaigner in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

From the start of his time in office, when a normally routine parliamentary vote to confirm him as chancellor turned into a humiliation requiring a second round of voting, Merz has struggled to establish his authority.

There have been repeated gaffes, from saying people in Germany needed to work longer hours to identifying as "middle class" while working as a highly remunerated board member of BlackRock Asset Management.

Surveys indicate that his communication lapses and his difficulty in establishing an emotional connection with voters anxious about their economic future both contributed to the outcome of all five state elections this year.
But Germany's deep-seated economic challenges — an ageing population, poor growth and the erosion of its industrial base under increasing pressure from China — resist easy solutions.

The reforms themselves caused problems in formerly communist eastern Germany, where despite more than three decades of economic transformation, more voters than in the west earn the minimum wage and rely completely on the state pension in retirement.

Manuela Schwesig, the SPD state premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, whose success in limiting the AfD's gains in her state was one of the few bright spots for the government, said she was "surprised" by Merz's refusal to change course.
Her campaign was heavily critical of Merz, whom she accused of showing indifference towards voters struggling with soaring fuel prices.

She also called for changes to the pension reform that would require people to work for longer — a particularly unpopular issue in the east, where many have not built up the same level of savings as those in the west.

Days before the vote, as speculation grew that his position might be in danger, senior CDU leaders rallied around the chancellor, aware that replacing him would put the reform programme at risk without solving underlying problems.
So far, the policy — known as the 'firewall' — under which the mainstream parties refuse to cooperate with the AfD has kept it from sharing power.
But there are growing doubts about whether it is possible to exclude a party which enjoys the support of more voters in Germany than any other.
Despite reservations about cooperating with a party with elements that are classified by the domestic security services as extremist right-wing, there are growing calls in the CDU for a rethink.
"This 'firewall' hasn't done anything for the CDU and they need to think about that," said Leif-Erik Holm, the AfD's lead candidate in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

Opinion polls have shown deep disillusion among many voters with a political system that has seen a succession of coalitions between the formerly fiercely antagonistic mainstream parties of the centre-right and centre-left.
Under former Chancellor Angela Merkel, the "grand coalition" of CDU and SPD, seen only once before at federal level during the 1960s, became standard.
Merz, once seen as a firebrand conservative, repeated the exercise after another coalition, headed by SPD Chancellor Olaf Scholz, collapsed in 2024.
"It's just allowed a vacuum on the right and the left for these parties to emerge," David-Wilp said.
* The writer is from Reuters

a47338e7e5e73fff: AYER KEROH: With the dissolution of the Melaka state legislative assembly expected to be announced tomorrow, Chief Minister Datuk Seri Ab Rauf Yusoh has left three key messages to ensure continuity in the state's development efforts.
The three messages are to uphold integrity, use artificial intelligence (AI) wisely and make the Melaka Sayang Rakyat (MeSRa) agenda the heart of public service.
He said positions held by civil servants were not a privilege but a trust that must be carried out responsibly to maintain public confidence in the civil service.
"Do not let one wrong decision tarnish your own name and cause the people's trust in the entire civil service to be affected.
"If we hold the people's trust, we must never trade it away," he said in his speech at the Melaka State Public Service Workers Appreciation Night.
Also present were state legislative assembly Speaker Datuk Ibrahim Durum, state secretary Datuk Salhah Salleh and senior state executive councillor Datuk Rais Yasin.
Rauf said civil servants must also be prepared to embrace technological developments by using AI to improve the efficiency of service delivery to the people.
"I want Melaka civil servants to use AI to work faster, more accurately and better.
"But remember, use AI to help us think, not to replace our thinking," he said.
For his third message, he urged all civil servants to make MeSRa the heart of their responsibilities and service to the community.

He said the effectiveness of a government should not be measured solely by the slogans or policies it promotes, but by people's experience when dealing with the government and how effectively their problems were resolved.
"Because ultimately, the people do not judge the government by the slogans we proclaim, but by the treatment they receive and the problems we solve," he said.
Rauf said the spirit of togetherness among civil servants must be maintained to ensure the state administration continued to function effectively in the people's interest.
He said if he was entrusted to continue leading the state administration, he hoped the spirit of togetherness would be preserved.
"We will continue what is good, improve what is lacking and, most importantly, ensure the state administration continues to move forward for the people and for Melaka," he said.
He also expressed his appreciation to all civil servants who played a key role in ensuring the state government's agendas and programmes were implemented.

They included staff from the Management Services Division of the Melaka Chief Minister's Department, Tourism Promotion Division of the State Communications, Multimedia and Tourism Committee, Technical and Logistics Division, as well as members of the media in Melaka.

"My media friends, I know they are the hardest to admit when they are tired. Not only do they have to rush to my programmes from morning until night, but wherever I go now, whenever there is a press conference, there is always one question being asked: Datuk Seri, when are you dissolving the state assembly?

"I go to a programme, they ask. I visit a village, they ask again. Even if they see me walking a little faster, they might think I am on my way to announce the dissolution! Just be patient until the time comes. I will know what to do," he said.

24f7b85df690e679: KUALA LUMPUR: National women's hockey coach C.R. Kumar was disappointed with his side after they struggled to beat minnows Bangladesh 3-1 for their second straight Group A win at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games in Gifu today.

World No. 21 Malaysia failed to establish control against their 85th-ranked opponents, falling behind in the 25th minute to a Kona Akter goal. The Speedy Tigresses, however, recovered in the second half through a brace from Nuramirah Shakira Zulkifli in the 40th and 59th minutes, alongside a 44th-minute strike by Zati Alyani Zubir.
The victory follows Malaysia's 5-0 win over Kazakhstan on Sept 18.
"We kept pressing them, but we were not clinical. Bangladesh, meanwhile, were quick on the counter," said Kumar.
"We also did not expect Bangladesh to perform well," he said, adding that his side's tendency to concede early goals remains a major issue.
Kumar was also unhappy with the team's penalty corner conversion rate, as they managed to convert only one of their seven opportunities, while also failing to convert a penalty stroke.
"We need to play much better in the match against powerhouse China," he added.
Malaysia face defending champions and world No. 4 China on Wednesday.

China, who won silver at the 2024 Paris Olympics and claimed the Asia Cup title in Gongshu last year — where they routed Malaysia 8-0 in the group stage — have had a dominant start, thrashing Bangladesh 13-0 and Taiwan 10-0 in their opening two matches.
China, coached by Australian Alyson Annan, will be seeking maximum points against Malaysia to secure a semi-final spot.

7c3db1c62d463633: Today, I’m talking with Mark Gurman, who is the world’s best-sourced Apple reporter — both as Bloomberg’s chief Apple correspondent and the host of the upcoming podcast Power On.
Earlier this month, Apple hosted its annual iPhone hardware event, virtually every detail of which was reported ahead of time by Mark. But this event was special, for a number of reasons.

It was new Apple CEO John Ternus’ first major product launch since he took over for former CEO Tim Cook less than two weeks prior. It was also the debut of the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable smartphone. The timing of those two things was not at all coincidental, as you’ll hear Mark explain. Apple takes these hardware events — and the stories they tell — extremely seriously.

This year’s story actually says a great deal about what’s happening at Apple, how Cook managed in wholesale leadership ranks over the past year, and how all of that might change Apple’s culture. Furthermore, what all that tells about Ternus’ plan to navigate Apple from what you might call the iPhone era into the AI era.
Okay: Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman on the future of Apple. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Mark Gurman, you’re the chief Apple correspondent and the managing editor of consumer technology at Bloomberg. Welcome to Decoder.
Good to be here finally. Thanks for having me. And it’s been a while, so it’s good to catch up on all things Apple.

Yeah, I’m really excited to talk to you. Obviously, Apple just had its big event. They announced the iPhone Duo. It was John Ternus’s first event as CEO. This is a Decoder episode, so we’ve got a new CEO, and we’ve got a new org chart inside of Apple.
There’s been a lot of shuffling. You’ve been chronicling them very, very deeply over the past few years. Let’s just start with the event. I have a very basic question for you.
Sure.
Do you ever get nostalgic for a time when you didn’t know what was going to happen at the iPhone event?
Do I ever get nostalgic?
Do you ever wish that you, Mark Gurman, were about to be surprised?

Honestly, I never think about it that way. I’m just fixated on delivering the goods and delivering the news. And people love their Apple. People want to know everything that’s coming down to the last minute, so I’m here to provide it for them.

The thing with me, and I don’t know if most people know this about me, but I hope people know this about me, is that I’m a huge Apple fan through and through, and I’ve always been. And I’m so lucky to be able to cover a company that I love, a company that I am obsessed with, and a company whose products I use. There are so many people who cover companies that they couldn’t care less about. That’s not me.

So I do what I do because I love Apple and I love covering Apple. I love the community around it, and I love talking about it. And it’s always fun to get a peek at the future and help keep not only myself informed, but people informed around me.
That actually leads me to a lot of things because I’ve known you forever. We’ve been working in and around the same spaces forever. You got your start as an Apple blogger at the Apple rumor sites.

There’s a whole culture around Apple that has grown up and changed over the years, and you can trace it to different eras of hardware, to different CEOs, to different sizes of the company. This was the first event with John Ternus as CEO. Apple announced a big new product in the iPhone Duo.
Do you sense that the community is changing? How do you think that community has changed over the years? And do you think Ternus is going to lead to a difference in what that community feels like?

I have to say, this event really didn’t feel much different than a Tim Cook event. They felt pretty interchangeable. It could have been Tim up there introducing it. It could have been Ternus up there introducing it.

The one thing I will say that did feel slightly different is that Ternus came out swinging with a point of view on AI. The first thing he came out with was about the intelligent personal hub. Now, here’s the big difference between Tim Cook and John Ternus in terms of their management style. You’re inside Apple, you’re an executive, you’ll come to him with an idea, you’ll come to him with a viewpoint, a decision, an opinion, and he’ll just pepper you with more questions. He won’t make a singular decision in many cases. It’s very much communal decision-making, collaborative decision-making.

John Ternus, if you come to him and you want him to make a decision, he’ll make a decision. He’ll have an opinion. Now, you may hate his opinion; you may completely disagree with him, but he has a viewpoint. But that’s the big difference between talking to people about Ternus and Tim.

Ternus comes out talking about his view on AI. I may disagree with it. A lot of people may disagree with it. They may think the OpenAI or Anthropic approach is superior, but at least he came out and had a viewpoint.

Apple’s been at this AI game now for two years since they launched Apple Intelligence at WWDC in 2024, and it’s been a mishmash of things. They haven’t really come out with a very strong narrative and viewpoint, and they finally did. So, as I said, whether you agree with it or not, they did do that. And I thought that was a really interesting way to kick off the keynote.
All right, we’re just going to get into the weeds of Apple nerds disagreeing about things.
Okay, let’s do it.

I sat through that event, and I appreciated the same thing that you saw, which is, “Oh, we’re telling a story.” John Ternus is on the stage, and the first thing he’s doing is telling a story about this product and how it fits into the universe of technology. And then I took a beat, and I was like, oh, but they’re also just making sure that he’s successful at his first event by playing Apple’s greatest hits.
Because an “intelligent personal hub” is just a replay of Steve Jobs saying the iMac was the digital hub. At the very end of the event, Ternus said, “There’s one more thing, and it’s the iPhone Duo.”

There was just a part of all of that that, to me, felt like Apple saying, “Look, our new CEO can put on the clothes of the old CEO. He can do this same dance that you’re expecting.” Underneath it, what I felt was, to your point, that I don’t buy the story about the intelligent hub.
No, I don’t buy it either.
Because any of the things we’re seeing AI do are happening in cloud services. It’s the same week that Meta launched Muse, right?
Right.

You can feel what you want about Meta launching Muse, but Mark Zuckerberg is giving everybody 8GB of storage and 8GB of RAM in the cloud, and Muse can go do a lot of things that AI on the iPhone absolutely cannot do at this point in time.

I just felt like there was a part where they were playing it really safe with John by having him basically show up and be the new lead singer of Journey. You can’t get it wrong if you’re going to do “Lights.” If you’re going to show up on stage and do “Don’t Stop Believin’,” you’re going to be fine for a minute. And it’s all the stuff that comes after that’s going to really show his real personality. But it sounds like you thought that that’s his point of view.

Well, it’s a couple of things. At a very high level, Apple’s going to tell a story around what they have. If Apple invented ChatGPT, they would’ve invented ChatGPT, and they would’ve told a good story around that. Apple has gone as far as it’s able to, at least for now, on AI. So it’s telling the story, the best version of that story that they can with what they have to work with, with the bird they have in hand. So that’s the one thing.

I agree with you on the intelligent personal hub, and how that compares to the iMac back in ’98. And it feels like they’re trying to sell this pivot from the Mac as the center of everything with the peripherals around it; then you got to iCloud in 2011, the center of everything with the peripherals around it. Now, it’s this Intelligence right at the center with everything around it.

But what’s so fascinating is that Apple held a major product launch event in September of the year 2026 and did not introduce a single notable new AI feature. The first 15 minutes or so of the keynote was simply a replay, a re-narrativization of what they introduced over the past two years with Apple Intelligence. And so they tried to just tell that story in a more concrete way.

The other thing is they don’t have any AI devices at the very core, and so they need to prop up the iPhone as their AI device because they don’t have an alternative. But of course they’re only going to do that until they have that killer device, and then they’re going to change that whole narrative.

So it’s a very narrative PR and marketing-driven company. And I’m not saying that to be critical. I mean, if I ran the company, obviously I’m going to tout what I have. I’m not going to veer from that. But it is interesting how they’re playing this. And I agree, they did play it very safe. There’s nothing safer than John Ternus introducing a new iPhone. It’s like the safest thing you can do. No major new AI product, no smart home hub, nothing in the spatial space, just straight down the middle.
Yeah, it seems like that next wave of smart home products, which we’re expecting later this year… I say, “We’re expecting.” I’m expecting it because that is something you have reported.
[Laughs] I am expecting it, yes.

Mark Gurman is expecting new products from Apple. That is the first cut at some truly AI-native devices. Because you have Siri AI and it is functional now in a way that it previously was not functional, you can try some new classes of devices.

There are about a half dozen AI-native devices coming in the next year and a half or so. The first will be the smart home hub, which is basically an Amazon Echo Show but Apple-style. It will have a square screen and an entirely new operating system. The idea is: what would a Siri AI operating system look like? This is that: intercom, video conferencing, proactive intelligence.

So you walk up to it, it recognizes who you are, and it will show content personal to you. It will know who is speaking. Obviously, the Amazon Echo can do that, but Apple’s doing it in its own Apple-y way with AI-based Face ID.

They’re working on a home security system. They’re working on another version of the smart home hub that I just talked about that is attached to a robotic arm. So you put it on your desk, and it can move around. It’s actually a category that’s pretty popping in Asia and in China right now.

Then you’ve got the wearables, the smart glasses. I still believe those are going to be introduced and shipped in 2027, so not too far from now. Trust me, you’ll be wearing them. Within 365 days, you will be wearing them and have video footage of you wearing them at the Steve Jobs Theater. And if that is not the case, either something went horribly wrong for you or something went horribly wrong for Apple.
You’ll also have the AirPods with cameras. That’s an interesting thing that we should talk about, but they’ll have the AirPods with cameras and then a few other wearables that I won’t get into.

So this is what I was talking about when I said there were eras at Apple and people’s relationship with the company really changed. The Steve Jobs era was defined by devices, and in particular, Steve Jobs himself getting up and doing a keynote and famously putting up pictures of all the existing smartphones and saying, “Well, these all suck. And here’s the reason they all suck, and here’s the iPhone and here’s why it’s better.”

That created one kind of relationship between Apple’s enormous community of fans, its leader, and the products. I think that was very successful. I think the Tim Cook era has been meaningfully different. I think it’s largely a story about scale. To some extent, it’s a story about values. To a huge extent, it’s a story about privacy.

Apple has marketed itself as the privacy company. It fought the FBI to keep the iPhone encrypted. There’s a lot there with Tim Cook’s version of the company, but it’s more corporate. Certainly, it’s just a vaster company. It’s safer. It’s not as rough around the edges as Jobs’ Apple, but it wasn’t as device-based.

I don’t think the Vision Pro has the same kind of mainstream cultural impact as even the hockey puck mouse that Jobs put out. There was a thing that he could do with products that Tim Cook Apple could not quite do with products. And that just feels really different to me.

I’m going to correct you on that because every time I put an article or a post out about the Vision Pro being on life support, I get what amounts to basically a notch or two below a death threat from dozens of people. So people are passionate about it.
Dozens? Dozens?

Well, honestly, I think what it is is that people have created businesses around spatial computing and apps, and they’re just pissed off that they’ve invested all this time and money in a category that’s probably going to die out.

And then you have consumers who spent four grand on this product, and they’re like, “I saved up for this thing, I’m living with this thing, and I’m pissed off to hear the realities.” But if you have another hour, we can talk about the Vision Pro.

No, the comparison there is good. People have invested in it. They care deeply about it. The comparison I’m making is that the relationship people have to Apple in the Cook era is as an institution. It’s just like this big thing that spans the globe on a massive scale.
It’s IBM.

Yeah, and in the Jobs era, it was all about really, really innovative new products that redefined categories over and over again. You’re describing a whole bunch of new products that came up in the Cook era that John Ternus is going to launch. How do you expect the culture of Apple to change around its products or its relationship to the culture to change as we go from one CEO to another?

But think about what they did. You’ve got the coolest new iPhone and Apple product in maybe 10, 20 years introduced one week after Tim Cook steps down. And then for the next 12 to 18 months, you’ve got, I don’t know, six or seven new product categories. Maybe you have 25 pretty breakthrough things.

So Tim Cook made a decision that, even though his tenure at a product company was pretty limited in major new things, the Apple Watch turned out to be a success, even though it started as a complete dud, as you remember. The AirPods are a unique beast in that they’re an accessory, but it’s not a platform on its own yet. It’s going to get there. And the Vision Pro is a failure.

Tim Cook could have ended his tenure as CEO with the iPhone Duo. He could have just waited. Typical transitions at Apple happen mid-October or mid-April; they happen on January 1st. It was a specific decision that was made for John Ternus to be the one to introduce the iPhone Duo. It was a specific decision made for John Ternus to be the one to introduce this whole new product roadmap. Even though, as you know, because of the length of hardware development cycles and R&D, these things were in the oven for five to 10 years.

So it’s really interesting that this decision was made to let Ternus be the face of this whole new era of products rather than allow Tim Cook to take the credit for it. And I think that’s to your point where they’re trying to draw the line in the sand of this new era. If Cook is already going to step down in the next three years, let’s just do it now and let Ternus take the credit for everything.

Take me inside that. You’ve obviously done a lot of reporting. I think you were the first to break the news that Cook would be searching for a successor. You were, I think, among the very first to break that it would be Ternus. Tell me about that process.

This is a big decision; Cook is going to play a huge role at the company. He has a massive compensation program tied pretty much to having to talk to Xi Jinping and Donald Trump. It seems like that’s his job: to just manage that relationship.
For $47 million a year, I would talk to Trump and Xi Jinping on the phone every day.

[Laughs] I would need at least 50, but that’s just me. That’s his job: to go do politics much the same way that Eric Schmidt at Google was in charge of governments after Larry Page became CEO. There’s a whole pattern here.
Brad Smith at Microsoft, even though he wasn’t CEO, but yeah.

He’s the president of the company. Yeah, there’s a parallel here. Tell me about this decision of Tim Cook wanting to elevate his position to something like that, and of making John Ternus the face of the product side of the company in this new role.

So 2023 rolls around and Tim Cook starts every executive team meeting, all high-level meetings with people at Apple at the executive levels, with, “We need to start taking succession seriously. We need to start thinking about who the next people are.” At that time, there was a really strong realization that many of the people at the top of Apple either had half a billion dollars in the bank or were already billionaires, and that this era would start to age out really quickly.

And so Tim Cook knew that he wanted to take a step back. Jeff Williams, the number two as the COO, knew he wanted to retire. The CFO, Luca Maestri, wanted to retire, too. The general counsel, Kate Adams, also wanted to retire. They were all about the same age, give or take a few years. So they basically came up with this plan that would go one by one over the next few years.

It started with the CFO. Luca retires at the very end of 2024, and he’s replaced by the new CFO, Kevan Parekh. Then 2025 rolls around, and Jeff Williams, the COO, retires and is replaced by his deputy, Sabih Khan. Then in 2026, they had the transition for the general counsel, and they got a great replacement for her from Meta, Jennifer Newstead. And then at the end of 2026, the big one: Tim Cook to John Ternus. So they played this out very, very slowly.

What Tim Cook has done, and I do think this is going to change in the Ternus era as we progress here, is that he came up with this strategy that I call “Hotel California.” You never want to leave. Tim Cook, he’s staying around as executive chairman. The general counsel had her stay around an extra six to nine months to run government affairs. Jeff Williams stayed around three to four months after stepping down as COO to just oversee the design team, the watch team, and the health teams as part of a transition.

For CFO Luca Maestri, the vast majority of his responsibilities went to his successor, but he kept three things. He kept oversight of information systems and technology. It’s basically like your IT department, corporate information security — which is security for the organization — and corporate real estate, so campuses, retail stores, facilities, and whatnot. It was kind of a BS job, I’ll be honest with you.

It was more so keeping him on the payroll and keeping him around in case things hit the fan, they had a financial issue, and they needed the adult or the grandfather in the room to take the bull by the horns and fix things as they transitioned to the new guy. But now Luca, he’s still there, still getting paid, and he’s teaching a class once a week at Apple University. So he’s a professor there now. 453053b2ec3ebe43: Amazon has blocked Meta's new Muse AI agent from shopping on its website, apparently deciding that having someone else's bot wandering through customer accounts and placing orders is a step too far. The ecommerce giant cut off Muse after unsuccessfully asking Meta to prevent the personal AI agent from accessing its store, GeekWire reported. Users who try anyway are told that access by an "unauthorized AI agent" violates Amazon's Conditions of Use. The Register asked Muse to find the "best-reviewed ergonomic office chair," add it to our cart, and proceed to the final checkout screen. Muse reported: "Hit a snag: Amazon is showing an anti-bot wall that blocks automated browsers outright – the browser couldn't even get to the search page, so no chair was found or added. I didn't push past it, since the notice says continuing would violate Amazon's terms." Meta launched Muse in the US earlier this month as an agent capable of doing more than answering questions. It can act on a user's behalf by shopping, making payments, reading emails, and managing calendars. When a service does not provide a public API, Meta says Muse can operate it through a browser much as a human would. Amazon is not keen on that arrangement. The retailer told GeekWire that Meta had neither informed it that Muse would access the store nor obtained authorization. It also claimed that the agent fails to identify itself while browsing and appears to capture and store customer credentials. Amazon said Muse could also access account information, including a customer's order history, when instructed to do so. Meta says the Muse model cannot see users' passwords or payment methods. Credentials are instead held in secure storage and made available for authentication without being exposed to the model. The Register asked Meta for further comment. Account security is not the only issue at stake. Amazon has spent much of the past year trying to keep rival AI agents away from its storefront. It took Perplexity to court over the Comet browser and has also moved to block shopping agents from Google and OpenAI. Amazon, of course, has shopping agents of its own. Alexa for Shopping researches products and makes recommendations, while Buy for Me purchases goods from other retailers' websites on a customer's behalf. Amazon says the latter identifies itself to those retailers and allows them to opt out. The company also has a financial reason to control the shopping trip: advertising. Amazon generated more than $68 billion in advertising revenue last year, helped by shoppers visiting its properties and viewing the products and sponsored placements displayed there. If outside AI agents take over product discovery, comparison, and purchasing, fewer shoppers may see Amazon's advertising or interact with its recommendation systems. Amazon is all-in on agentic shopping – provided it is Amazon's agent holding the credit card. ® An Amazon spokesperson told The Reg: “We think it’s fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate. "This helps ensure a safe, secure, and reliable customer experience, and it is how others operate including food delivery apps and the restaurants they take orders for, delivery services apps and the stores they shop from, and online travel agencies and the airlines they book tickets with for customers. Agentic third-party applications such as Muse have the same obligations, and we’ve requested that Meta remove Amazon from the experience.”
c129a32d44ff756d: NAGOYA: Schoolgirl swimmer Yu Zidi won her second gold of the Asian Games on Monday with the fastest time in the world this year, while a teenage badminton player became the first doping case.

North Korea led through Chae Un Yong's first-half goal.
Yun Su-jeong's second-half strike ensured the spoils were shared and the players exchanged tepid high-fives at the end, but did not speak to each other.
The neighbours remain technically at war because the 1950-53 Korean war ended with an armistice rather than a peace treaty.

The boxing began Monday at Aichi's Nishio Gymnasium with some shock results in the men's light-middleweight (70kg) as silver and bronze medallists from three years ago at the Hangzhou Games both lost in the last 32.
Kan Chia-wei of Taiwan, second in Hangzhou, was beaten on a 4-1 split decision by Palestine's Mohammed Issa.
"I am not satisfied with this result," said Kan. "I suffered a shoulder injury, so my next goal is to regain my fitness."
That came moments after Bayramdurdy Nurmuhammedov of Turkmenistan, third in 2023, lost by the same scoreline to Bahrain's Aly Abdalla.
"He doesn't have IQ, he just (puts) pressure, pressure, pressure," said Abdalla after outthinking his marauding opponent.

Palestine, who have experienced war in Gaza since October 2023, made their debut in Asian Games baseball.
Though they lost 12-0 to the Philippines their team leader said that just being there "was a win."
"With everything that's going on, what we are trying to do is bring hope to people who do not have a lot of it," said Oney Roberto Guillen Cardenas.
"Just by us being out there on the same stage as countries like Japan ... that's a win in itself."
Hasan Ammar, who registered his team's first hit, said: "This is probably the greatest honour of my life, playing for something so meaningful and on such a big stage.

bc6f3c4554d3ead5: SUKAU, Sept 21 — Deep in Malaysia’s Borneo jungle, wild shouts fill the air as a Bornean elephant is darted and her angry herd rallies to protect her.

The downed elephant is one of only around 1,000 Bornean elephants left in the wild, and the team that darted her is working to protect the endangered species by minimising growing conflict between the animals and local communities.
Once the herd has been chased off, conservationist Farina Othman and her team move in to attach a tracking collar to the animal.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

This photo taken on August 24, 2026, shows Farina measuring the length of a female Bornean elephant’s leg during a GPS collaring operation as part of a collaboration involving several agencies near the Kinabatangan River in Sukau. — AFP pic
The collar allows them to alert villagers if the elephant strays too near.
It is also key to a programme Farina is designing to create “corridors” for elephants roaming a fragmented landscape of virgin forest patches, hemmed in by vast oil palm plantations and villages.
Farina has studied these elephants for years, earning her the nickname “Borneo’s elephant whisperer” as well as the prestigious Whitley Award for conservationists.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photo taken on August 25, 2026, shows a wild female Bornean elephant with a GPS collar around her neck crossing the Kinabatangan River in Sukau. — AFP pic
“It’s Pigtail,” she whispered, stroking the tranquilised elephant’s trunk and nodding to the distinctive tail that prompted its nickname.
The team works fast — the dart’s sedative effects last only half an hour, and the herd can still be heard nearby. Overhead, there are flashes of lightning as a tropical thunderstorm approaches.
As soon as the collar is securely fastened and blood samples are taken, the team, accompanied by AFP journalists, retreat into the forest before Pigtail rouses.
‘Conflict inevitable’
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photo taken on August 25, 2026, shows a herd of wild Bornean elephants crossing the Kinabatangan River in Sukau. — AFP pic

For the past 40 years, Bornean elephants have lost more than 60 per cent of their habitat in Sabah, in northern Borneo, to logging and, later, oil palm expansion, according to the International Union for Conservation of Nature, which listed the animal as endangered in 2024.
Lower Kinabatangan, a floodplain in eastern Sabah of around 400 square kilometres, is home to around 160 elephants.
But “only half of that is now a space left for the elephants,” said Farina, a Malaysian academic who heads local conservation group Seratu Aatai, or “Solidarity” in the local Sungai language.
When the animals venture into private property or nearby villages, “conflict is inevitable”, she told AFP.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

This aerial photo taken on August 26, 2026, shows a general view with the Kinabatangan River and surrounding jungle in Sukau, a small village near Sandakan in Sabah state on the island of Borneo. — AFP pic
In a recent incident, a herd of 20 elephants stomped into palm oil smallholdings and three villages, terrifying residents.
No one was injured, but the incident prompted calls for stronger deterrents, including upgraded electric fencing.
“People don’t feel safe around elephants, and that’s when conflict happens,” Farina said.
The animosity worsens when the animals, especially adventurous bulls, which can weigh up to five tonnes, cleverly bypass electric fencing to feast on palm trees or saplings.
That is why Farina and her team of 17 conservationists prioritise coexistence.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A herd of wild Bornean elephants crossing the Kinabatangan River in Sukau. — AFP pic
“We’re working to increase people’s tolerance, to increase connectivity space for elephants and to find a long-term solution,” she said.

Based in Sukau, a hamlet on the crocodile-infested banks of the Kinabatangan river, Seratu Aatai runs an outreach programme in plantation schools, distributes information pamphlets and has designated “community wildlife guardians” who help usher away elephants that have wandered into human habitation.
“Before, we didn’t know how to manage living near them,” said homestay owner Firah Kazenn, 21, who recently encountered elephants behind her home in Sukau.
“The elephants were unmonitored, and many were lost to conflict. Now, with the Seratu Aatai unit, they are protected, and the community is actively involved too,” Firah told AFP.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photo taken on August 27, 2026, shows boats docked along the shore of the Kinabatangan River and surrounded with jungle in Sukau. — AFP pic
“We’ve learnt safe ways to guide the elephants away when they come too close to our homes, without harming them,” she added.
‘Win-win situation’
Farina believes the best way to protect the animals is by creating “elephant corridors” — pathways through plantations connecting patches of habitat.
She is hoping to convince seven plantations in the area that elephants are “an ecological reality, rather than an occasional disturbance”.
But it will be a challenge.

Fierce competition driven by tight, volatile margins means many producers are not keen to sacrifice land for corridors, said Muhammad Al Shafieq bin Mustafa, a former plantation manager in Sukau and now a palm oil industry specialist.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Members of the team led by Farina measuring the length of a female Bornean elephant during a GPS collaring operation as part of a collaboration involving several agencies near the Kinabatangan River in Sukau. — AFP pic

“Those plantations that do commit and are willing to work with people like Farina often do not get the recognition that they deserve or the financial support that they need, especially from Western palm oil buyers,” he told AFP.
Industry-funded conservation associations say plantations have made progress in becoming sustainable palm oil producers but face difficult economic realities.
“It needs to be a win-win situation between the planters and also the wildlife,” said Daniel Pamin, conservation and sustainability executive at the Malaysian Palm Oil Green Conservation Foundation.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

This photo taken on August 24, 2026, shows Nabila Sarkawi, a veterinary officer with the Sabah Wildlife Department at Sepilok (back), watching Khairun Amlan (right) administering a multivitamin injection during a GPS collaring operation led by Farina (unseen) as part of a collaboration involving several agencies near the Kinabatangan River in Sukau. — AFP pic
Farina believes change will come.
Before, locals used the Malay word “halau”, meaning “chase away” or “banish”, when talking about elephants.
“Now, we are working to get people to say... ‘walking’ or ‘escorting’ out the elephant.” — AFP
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A wild male Bornean elephant crossing the Kinabatangan River with a plastic bag wrapped around its trunk in Sukau. — AFP pic
7eb6a763d30f63b4: ISLAMABAD, Sept 21 — Pakistani teenager Zara Shah was targeted by a stranger while playing a computer game, drawn into a conversation that would expose her to terrifying online sexual exploitation.

Zara, whose name has been changed by AFP for safety reasons, is one of an estimated 1.5 million children in Pakistan who experienced online sexual abuse in one year, according to a report published by the UN children’s agency this month.
“We started chatting while playing an online game, and he began acting like a friend. Later, he wanted to meet and, after, started asking me for nudes,” 17-year-old Shah said.
“When I refused, he threatened to find my family online and tell them that we had been talking,” she added.
According to the Unicef report, around 85 per cent of perpetrators were known to the victims, aged between 12 and 17.
“The abuse may start with a friendly conversation, a gaming interaction, a promise of gifts, money or romance,” Daniel Kardefelt, lead author of the global Unicef report, told AFP.
“Perpetrators may spend months building trust using information that they find on social media,” Kardefelt said.

In Muslim-majority Pakistan, 71 per cent of victims did not tell anyone, according to the Unicef report, while no child surveyed reported the abuse through formal channels — including police, helplines or social workers.
Their silence was mostly because of stigma, shame and fears over how their families or society may react.

“Around 44 per cent of reported abuse was entirely online, with Snapchat and WhatsApp among the most common settings,” said Mehek Naeem, director of Pahchaan, a children’s rights organisation based in the eastern city of Lahore.
Girls can face heightened risks of sexual extortion in the conservative society, which can lead to restrictions on their mobility or withdrawal from school.
For Zara, the threat of being exposed to her family was enough to keep her silent.
“I could have been stopped from going to school or leaving the house altogether,” she said.
“Staying quiet felt like the better option than speaking up. But anxiety kills me every day.”
Loopholes, ‘no implementation’
With around 74 per cent of children aged 12 to 17 in Pakistan estimated by Unicef to be internet users, concerns over online safety are growing as their access to digital platforms expands.
Echoing other policies around the world, the provincial government in Punjab this month passed a resolution to bar children under 16 from using social media.
However, it has faced opposition.
“I disagree with the ban,” said Usama Khilji, a digital rights activist.
“It will be a challenge to implement, and children can circumvent the ban through VPNs. Children have the right of freedom of expression, and a ban takes that away,” he said.
Pakistan has a legal framework addressing tech-facilitated offences against children, but “there is no implementation”, said Tahira Afrasiyab, a spokesperson for non-profit organisation Muslim Hands.
And, according to experts, there are loopholes in existing laws.

Human rights lawyer Salman Afridi said this issue shows how “economic vulnerability can be weaponised” for amounts as small as 10,000 Pakistani rupees (RM147) in exchange for the production of sexual content.
“What we are seeing is the use of technology to facilitate an entire chain of grooming, inducement, coercion, blackmail, production, distribution and commercialisation,” he said.
“There is a strong basis for describing this as a commercial ecosystem of exploitation,” Afridi added.
For Zara and many others like her, the consequences of an encounter that began with an online game remain difficult to escape.
“I was, and am, scared,” she said. “I live in fear.” — AFP
793467a1d7a7e161: WELLINGTON, Sept 21 — A record number of New Zealanders turned out at the polls this month, not for national elections but to vote for their Bird of the Year — the critically endangered black robin.
The diminutive native lives on the remote Chatham Islands, 800 kilometres (500 miles) off the South Island’s east coast.
In 1980, only five of the birds remained, including a single breeding female. Now there are about 350.
The black robin topped the pecking order ahead of the famed flightless parrot, the kakapo, and the native karearea falcon, which came in second and third.
The annual Bird of the Year competition is run by independent conservation organisation Forest and Bird, and has been the subject of significant controversy in the past decade.
In 2019 there were accusations of Russian interference after hundreds of votes were registered from IP addresses in the country.
Forest and Bird deemed most of the votes were legitimate, and said it did not affect the victory of the hoiho, or yellow-eyed penguin.
In 2023 the puteketeke won the title after receiving the celebrity backing of Last Week Tonight comedian John Oliver, who urged his viewers to vote for the lake dweller.
Forest and Bird’s Rebecca Hatch said voter numbers had soared this year, but not due to foreign interference.
“This year has seen record numbers of votes with 105,000 people choosing their favourite,” Hatch said.
“New Zealanders have really shown up for nature. Roughly one in every 50 Kiwis voted,” she said, referring to the country’s people and not the native, flightless birds.
The black robin received more than 26,000 votes.
The Chatham Islands Landscape Restoration Trust ran the campaign for the black robin and is seeking to create a third habitat for the birds to expand their biodiversity. — AFP

dd1207301163a70c: Clop has discovered what life is like on the receiving end of an extortion demand after rival crew ShinyHunters hijacked its leak site and demanded an eight-figure payout. ShinyHunters told Reuters that it broke into the site on Friday by exploiting a vulnerability in the software powering it. The crew claimed this gave it extensive access to Clop's infrastructure. "We basically own them now," it said. Clop has not responded publicly, although two security researchers told Reuters that the clash appeared genuine. The Register has also viewed the defaced site, where ShinyHunters is posting increasingly colorful demands. According to ShinyHunters, the feud dates back to Clop's attacks on Oracle E-Business Suite (EBS) customers last year. In a message posted on September 19, ShinyHunters demanded an eight-figure payment, claiming the sum represented 2.333 percent of its own net worth. A later update raised the demand to "all the money you made off the EBS campaign plus more AND WITH INTEREST." ShinyHunters also threatened to identify companies that allegedly paid Clop and publish the sums and Bitcoin addresses involved. ShinyHunters turned the screw again on September 21, warning that its demands would increase with every 24 hours that Clop failed to respond. The gang has spent years exploiting vulnerabilities in enterprise software to steal data and extort victims, most notoriously during the 2023 MOVEit campaign, which affected thousands of organizations and exposed information belonging to tens of millions of people. Its latest target is rather more familiar with that business model than most. The potential damage to Clop goes beyond the defacement of its leak site. For now, though, those claims remain unverified. There is also the small matter of Clop's reputation. Leak sites are intended to demonstrate that an extortion crew has both the stolen goods and control of its operation. Having yours hijacked by a rival and repurposed to demand money from you is not exactly a glowing advertisement. ShinyHunters says the price will continue rising every 24 hours until Clop responds. 44fa64bc3c3f95fa: HONG KONG: Datuk Jackie Chan may be one of the world's biggest action icons, but there was a time when he was hardly considered leading-man material.
According to Hong Kong media reports, veteran filmmaker Ng See Yuen recently shared a brutal moment from Chan's early career that the action superstar never forgot.
Ng, who helped launch Chan's kung fu career, recalled an encounter involving Taiwanese actress Pearl Chang Ling, who was a huge star back in the 1970s.
At the time, the now 72-year-old Chan was still a struggling, relatively unknown actor.
Director Lo Wei was preparing a new film and had set his sights on Chang to play the female lead.
Hoping to pitch the project, Lo brought Chan along to her dressing room.
As Lo enthusiastically talked up the script, Chang, who was putting on her makeup in front of a mirror, casually asked who would play the male lead.
Lo pointed straight to Chan and said: "Him."
Chang reportedly took one look at Chan and scoffed: "Is someone like you even worthy of being paired with me?"
Years later, after Chan had achieved global stardom, Ng asked him if the snub actually happened.
Chan's answer was instant: "I'll remember it till the day I die!"
Chan's early years in the film industry were far from smooth.
His early movies struggled at the box office, and he was even mocked by renowned author Gu Long.
Even when director Yuen Woo-ping wanted to cast Chan in the 1978 action comedy Snake in the Eagle's Shadow, Ng—who produced the film—was initially unconvinced.
Pointing out Chan's poor box-office record, Ng favored another actor.
However, Yuen fought for Chan, and Ng eventually gave in, prepared to take the financial risk.
It proved to be a gamble that paid off handsomely. Snake in the Eagle's Shadow became a major box-office hit, launching Chan to stardom and cementing his place in cinema history.

8d5bd560f0b1aad2: MILAN: Hospital tests have ruled out drug use by Italy's Daniel Maldini when he was involved in a road accident in Milan this month, a local police source said on Monday.

24a0aba8852ada76: LONDON, Sept 21 — UK flights faced fresh disruption Monday, with some cancelled due to a technical issue at the nation’s air traffic control agency — the second such outage in two weeks.
The National Air Traffic Services (NATS), plagued by several incidents in recent years, apologised for the latest incident at a centre in Scotland that has since been fixed.
“We are working with airports and airlines to... minimise any further disruption,” NATS said in a statement.
It followed an outage on September 8 and 9, when a software glitch caused more than 2,000 UK flight cancellations and numerous delays, affecting more than 330,000 passengers.
“The issue at our Prestwick centre in Scotland... is unrelated to the issue two weeks ago,” said a NATS spokesperson.
In its latest update, aviation analytics firm Cirium said 72 out of more than 6,000 flights to or from the UK had been cancelled.
“If this were the end of the day... this level of cancellations is close to normal — around one per cent,” it noted in a statement.
“However, as it’s early in the day, we anticipate that operational performance will degrade quickly.”
It added that while Glasgow and Belfast had experienced “high cancellations... London-area airports are not particularly impacted”.
Transport minister Heidi Alexander acknowledged that the new incident, which she referred to on X as an “IT issue”, “will be deeply frustrating for passengers after the previous issue”.
Irish airline Ryanair once more called for the resignation of NATS chief executive Martin Rolfe — who received Downing Street’s backing following the incident earlier this month.
Europe’s biggest carrier by passenger numbers said more than 140 Ryanair flights had been delayed, leaving over 25,000 passengers facing delays.
The travel chaos earlier this month followed a technical glitch in July 2025 that saw scores of flights to and from the UK cancelled, prompting anger from airline chiefs.
Britain suffered its worst air systems failure in years in 2023, with more than 700,000 passengers affected after hundreds of flights were delayed or cancelled.
NATS has operated under a public-private partnership model since 2001. The government holds a 49-percent stake, as well as a “golden share” enabling it to intervene in strategic decisions.
The remainder is held primarily by a consortium of airlines. — AFP
b96363eae49d2157: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
The US spent billions on border surveillance. Why can’t it catch people before they die?

When José Morales Bernal crossed the border into the US in April 2024, the day before his 32nd birthday, he was within range of three surveillance towers equipped with cameras and AI to automatically detect and track people.
If the system worked as intended, Morales should have been apprehended. If he needed medical help, agents were trained to provide it. None of that happened.

Instead, Morales died just 360 feet from the closest tower. It was local landfill workers, rather than Border Patrol, who first spotted him. An autopsy concluded that he had died of “environmental exposure.”

A first-of-its-kind investigation by MIT Technology Review reveals that deaths like Morales’s are startlingly common. After mapping nearly 4,000 locations where human remains were found against information on nearly 600 surveillance towers, we discovered that a humanitarian crisis at the border has unfolded in view of the government’s own cameras.
Read our full investigation into the deadly failings of the virtual wall.
—James O’Donnell and Eileen Guo
Learn more:
As part of our 15-month investigation, we created the first comprehensive map of deaths near US-Mexico border surveillance towers. Take a look at that map, and read about how we made it.

The US government is about to spend another $1 billion to triple the virtual wall’s size, yet we found it has systemic flaws: broken towers, algorithms that failed to detect people and agents who simply did not respond to alerts. Here are four ideas for what Customs and Border Protection should do to rectify those failures.

An analysis by the Times of San Diego found at least 138 cases since 2022 in which migrants’ remains were found within the nominal range of a nearby surveillance tower. A separate MIT Technology Review analysis estimated that more than half of those people were likely within a tower’s field of view. Gómez Hernández was one of them. Here’s her story, written by our partners at Times of San Diego.
All of these stories are part of Dying on Camera, our new series investigating the failures of border surveillance technology and their human cost.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 An AI hallucination nearly triggered a US military operation A false report prompted plans to intercept a Chinese vessel. (CNN) + The incident comes as the Pentagon accelerates its use of AI. (Ars Technica) + “Humans in the loop” in AI war is an illusion. (MIT Technology Review)

2 Gemini has carried out Google’s first known autonomous AI hack Google says the behavior wasn’t “misaligned” because its safety measures caught it. (WSJ $) + Here’s why AI agents cheat to reach their goals. (MIT Technology Review)

3 The US has proposed an AI safety alert system with China It would flag AI incidents that pose national security risks. (AP) + Trump and Xi will consider the proposal at their summit this week. (NBC News) + Could AI really kill us all? (MIT Technology Review)

4 California’s governor has ordered work on an AI “kill switch” It’s part of Gavin Newsom’s executive order on AI safety. (NBC News) + The order also calls for independent oversight of AI companies. (NYT $)

5 Data centers are turning to forever chemicals for cooling PFAS cooling can reduce water use but raises pollution risks. (Fortune) + US regulators are fast-tracking PFAS for data center cooling. (The Hill)

6 Iran and China used AI agents to automate influence campaigns The agents created fake accounts and posts with little human input.(NYT $) + AI persuasion has entered elections. (MIT Technology Review)

7 Trump wants a new AI czar and an “AI Force” modeled on Space Force But he hasn’t said what the new force would do or where it would sit. (Axios) + The tech industry is scratching its head over the proposal. (Politico)
8 A cybercrime feud has erupted after a group hijacked a rival dark website The notorious ShinyHunters says it took control of cl0p’s site. (Reuters $)
9 Gambling giant DraftKings used AI to target “profitable losers” The model scored users on how they responded to promotions. (NYT $)
10 SpaceX’s next Starship flight will attempt its first orbital mission It will also deploy working Starlink V3 satellites. (New Scientist $)
Quote of the day
“There is 0% chance that’s going to be the end of the world.”
—Nvidia’s Jensen Huang dismisses warnings that AI could wipe out humanity by 2030 in an interview with CBS News.
One more thing
AI is pushing the limits of the physical world

Architecture often assumes a binary between built projects and theoretical ones. What physics allows in actual buildings is vastly different from what architects can imagine and design. But the latest advancements in AI have prompted a surge in the theoretical.

That shift was on display at an exhibition at Brooklyn’s Pratt Institute, which brought together works from more than 30 practitioners exploring AI’s experimental, generative and collaborative potential to open up new areas of architectural inquiry.
See how architects and designers are using AI to imagine what could be built.
—Allison Arieff
We can still have nice things

1f96853fb7a4b78a: KOTA TINGGI, Sept 21 — A five-year-old girl was found dead, believed to have been thrown into a river by her uncle in Kampung Padang, Tanjung Sedili here, this morning.

a3f9274478e73719: KUALA LUMPUR: Frontken Corporation Bhd's subsidiary, Ares Green Technology Corporation, is acquiring industrial land and the factory buildings erected thereon in Tainan City, Taiwan, from Ginwin Technology Co Ltd for RM118.16 million.

3172ad1ab4994406: PETALING JAYA: MCA vice-president Lawrence Low has urged the government to consider further raising the electricity bill protection threshold to 1,200 kWh per month.
Low said the government’s decision to raise the threshold from 600kWh to 800 kWh will provide households some immediate relief.

“However, the government needs to study extending the coverage to 1,200 kWh with a progressive mechanism so that households do not encounter a sudden sharp jump in their electricity bills once consumption exceeds the threshold,” he said in a statement.

Low, who is also the chairman of MCA's economic and SMEs affairs committee, said that under the current threshold, households that marginally exceed 800 kWh could face a sharp increase in their electricity bill.

“Relief should taper progressively as consumption rises, rather than disappear abruptly once a threshold is crossed. This would allow households to maintain normal electricity use while continuing to improve energy efficiency,” he said.
He said keeping electricity costs manageable did not mean encouraging waste.

“It gives households greater disposable income to invest in energy-efficient air conditioners, refrigerators, washing machines, computers, electric vehicles and other efficient technologies, thereby supporting the electrical, electronics, retail, repair and related service sectors,” he said.

On Thursday, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced that the government had raised the electricity bill protection threshold for domestic consumers from 600kWh to 800kWh per month, until the end of the year.
He said that under the revised measure, domestic consumers using up to 800kWh a month will be exempted from the Automatic Fuel Cost Adjustment (AFA), retail charges, and sales and service tax (SST).

Anwar, who is also the finance minister, previously said the haze and hot weather in recent weeks had led to increased electricity consumption among households, pushing their usage above the 600kWh threshold and exposing them to AFA charges.

Low called for a review of the 8% SST on household electricity to be reduced to 6% or lower, saying that if the government could lessen other taxes affecting essential services and economic activity, basic household electricity deserves similar consideration.

He also urged the government to review the current Regulatory Period 4 (RP4) base tariff, which determines the underlying electricity tariff, of 45.40 sen/kWh, and consider reducing it towards the 39.95 sen/kWh rate under the previous Regulatory Period 3 (RP3).
319479e4d0a223cb: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 21 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim held a nearly hour-long audience with Yang Dipertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, this evening, as a dispute over the status of the state executive council continued to unfold.
Anwar left Istana Negeri Sembilan in Changkat Persekutuan here after completing the audience, Astro Awani reported.
He had arrived at the palace grounds at about 6pm.
No details of the discussions during the meeting were immediately disclosed.
The audience came after Tuanku Muhriz revoked the appointments of the Negeri Sembilan State Executive Council members with immediate effect late last night.
According to a statement by Istana Negeri Sembilan comptroller Datuk Azizi Mohamad Ali, the decision was made after the ruler found that the exco members had breached their oaths of office.

The palace cited Article 38(5) of the Negeri Sembilan State Constitution 1959, which states that a member of the State Executive Council holds office for as long as he or she has the pleasure of the Yang di-Pertuan Besar.
The exco members had taken their oaths and signed pledges of loyalty on August 7 before being appointed to the council.
Negeri Sembilan Menteri Besar Datuk Ismail Lasim, however, disputed the validity of their removal in a statement today.
He said any action to dismiss or terminate the membership of an exco member without the advice or formal request of the Menteri Besar was “invalid, unconstitutional and had no legal effect”.
Ismail said he had not been consulted or provided advice on the removal of any exco member under Article 38(5).
He maintained there was therefore no need to submit a new list of proposed exco members, saying the existing line-up remained legally valid and would continue to carry out its duties as usual.
a69373ff0d656c88: PETALING JAYA, Sept 21 — Naturalised striker Bergson da Silva described his call-up to the Malaysian national team to compete in the Fifa Asean Cup 2026 in Indonesia from September 25 to October 5 as a dream come true after spending more than five years playing in the country with Johor Darul Ta’zim (JDT).

The Brazil-born striker said he never expected to get the opportunity to represent Malaysia, making his inclusion in the national squad a special moment for himself, his family and everyone who had supported his journey over the years.
“No, never. That’s why I told you, being here is like a dream for me, for my family and for all the people who have lived these moments with me during these more than five years.

“Representing this jersey and this country is a pleasure for all of us. We are here to give our best, and I am one of them,” he told reporters before the national team training session at Hilton Hotel here today.

Bergson, who has been among the top scorers in the M-League since joining JDT, said he viewed the responsibility of leading the Harimau Malaya attack as a major responsibility rather than pressure as he always determined to make the most of the opportunity to contribute to the team.

“Yes, I take it as a big and good responsibility, not as pressure. Every step that we take in life has targets, so being here is one more big responsibility for me. I always wanted to wear this jersey and be with the team. So, I just want to enjoy it and give my best,” he said.

Looking ahead to Malaysia’s meeting with Indonesia in the Fifa Asean Cup 2026, Bergson expects a tough encounter given the rivalry between the two sides and their respective ambitions to secure victory.

The Harimau Malaya squad will depart for Jakarta tomorrow to compete in the Division 1 of the Fifa Asean Cup 2026 competition after having been drawn in Group A alongside hosts Indonesia, Singapore and Bangladesh.
Group B comprises Vietnam, Thailand, the Philippines and Pakistan.
Malaysia, ranked 136th in the world, will open their campaign against 181st-ranked Bangladesh at Gelora Bung Karno, Jakarta on Friday.

The national side will then face 118th-ranked Indonesia at the same venue on September 28, before concluding their Group A campaign against 148th-ranked Singapore at Stadium Si Jalak Harupat, Bandung on October 1. — Bernama
00a0a119647a056d: AMSTERDAM: New Netherlands coach Xavi Hernandez wants more intensity from his team and for them to take the initiative in their Nations League matches this month, he said on Monday.

The former World Cup winner with Spain, who is also a former Barcelona coach, takes charge of his first match with the Dutch when they host Germany in Amsterdam on Thursday, followed by two games against Serbia and a trip to Greece in the expanded international window.
Xavi said he would be insisting on hard work and application from the 26-man squad, whom he was meeting for the first time on Monday.
“Everything is new for me and for the staff so it will first be to get to know each other, know all the players, insist or convince them about our way to play,” he told a press conference.
“We don't have too much time. But no excuses, every coach is in the same situation.

“I want to explain the values that we want from the squad. I want to show them that I'm open for them, I want to help them. I want to enjoy the process with them. We want to create a family, we want to create a big group. The players must come to the national team with happiness, but at the end, the main goal is to win.”
The Dutch had a disappointing World Cup with defeat in the last 32 by Morocco, after which Ronald Koeman resigned. He had been criticised for an overtly defensive approach.

“You cannot promise results but we will work for results. But I can promise that we will play with intensity, with passion, with a good rhythm, trying to be competitive and trying to be taking the initiative in the game. This for sure,” Xavi added.
“There's going to be a different way of playing. I don't want to compare, and I don't want to talk about the past. I respect Ronald a lot. But I'm focused on the present.”
Xavi said Virgil van Dijk would remain captain after the pair met in Liverpool to discuss his international future.
“It was a really good meeting. He was very honest. He has the capacity to continue. He's a good leader. He's positive, he's motivated. He's ready to be the leader.”
07f65790bab5a473: KUALA LUMPUR: Ranhill Utilities Bhd's shares hit an all time high on Monday, lifted by rising demand for industrial water infrastructure and Johor's data centre boom.

b8f8ea118557b69f: MADRID: Spain's World Cup-winning coach Luis de la Fuente is to sign a new contract keeping him in the role until 2032, the Spanish football federation (RFEF) announced on Monday.
"Luis de la Fuente will extend his contract through the next two European Championships, in 2028 and 2032, as well as the 2030 World Cup," the RFEF said in a statement.

527329cd16b05b42: KUALA LUMPUR: Financial markets are pricing a more hawkish US Federal Reserve interest rate path than the latest forecasts from policymakers and economists:
This could keep the US dollar supported into 2027, according to CIMB Securities Sdn Bhd.
The firm said markets are pricing about 80 basis points of additional Fed tightening in 2027, equivalent to roughly 3.2 rate hikes.
This is in comparison with the latest Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) projections for a 25-basis-point increase in the fourth quarter of 2026 and no further hikes in 2027.
The FOMC's latest projection puts the policy rate at 4.25 per cent after the expected fourth-quarter move.
CIMB Securities said market forecasts for end-2027 rates remain widely dispersed, ranging from 3.25 per cent to 4.50 per cent, with a median of 3.50 per cent.
The firm said near-term upside risks to global energy prices and potential price shocks could keep markets positioned for tighter US monetary policy in the fourth quarter of 2026.
It also revised higher its forecasts for US Treasury yields relative to German and Japanese government bonds.

CIMB Securities raised its end-2027 two-year US Treasury-Bund and US Treasury-JGB spread assumptions by eight basis points and 15 basis points to about 160 basis points and 270 basis points respectively.
The wider yield advantage is expected to support the dollar and reduce the case for sustained appreciation in the euro and yen.

CIMB Securities said a return of Brent crude to US$100 a barrel could provide another source of support for the dollar, particularly as higher energy prices tend to weigh on currencies of major energy importers.
The firm retained its near-term US Dollar Index (DXY) forecast at 101 but raised the third-quarter 2027 projection to 100.
However, a decline in Brent below US$90 a barrel could reduce that support, with the DXY ceiling estimated at 99.8 under a lower oil-price scenario.
For Asian currencies, CIMB Securities said the impact of higher US rates could be partly offset by relatively stable Chinese yuan conditions and higher regional yields.

It expects Asian currencies to remain within their 12-month forecast ranges, with potential yuan strength ahead of a China-US summit providing some stability for the ringgit, Singapore dollar and Thai baht.

Higher oil prices and US rates pose greater near-term risks to the Indonesian rupiah, they said, potentially adding pressure for a 25-basis-point Bank Indonesia rate hike in the fourth quarter of 2026.

668480c461016fd4: NASA has added almost $1 billion to SpaceX's commercial crew contract for three more Crew Dragon missions to the International Space Station (ISS). SpaceX has said it ultimately intends to retire Dragon and Falcon 9 in favor of Starship, assuming it can get the vastly larger vehicle operating reliably. NASA plans to retire the ISS around 2030 and use a SpaceX-developed vehicle to perform its controlled deorbit. NASA lists mission readiness dates in 2027 and 2028, with the contract's period of performance running through 2030. NASA awarded CCtCap contracts to SpaceX and Boeing in 2014. SpaceX has since flown numerous crews to the ISS. Boeing, not so much. The aviation giant's calamity capsule, Starliner, finally carried two astronauts to the outpost in 2024. They remained there until a SpaceX Crew Dragon brought them home after NASA decided that returning them aboard the Boeing vehicle posed too much risk. Starliner later returned safely to Earth without a crew. If these missions prove to be Crew Dragon's last hurrah, NASA and its partners will face a challenge in maintaining crewed access to low Earth orbit and the commercial stations planned to succeed the ISS. A report from NASA's Office of Inspector General identified multiple problems with the Starliner program and faulted both Boeing and the agency. SpaceX has had problems of its own, not least the explosion of a Crew Dragon capsule during ground testing in 2019. Starliner nevertheless earned its calamity capsule nickname through repeated uncrewed test failures and a 2024 Crew Flight Test that ended with the spacecraft returning without its astronauts. Despite the billions spent on Starliner, there is no guarantee that it will ever enter regular crew rotation service. Crew Dragon, meanwhile, could be approaching the end of its run, with one of these newly ordered flights potentially carrying the final astronauts to or from the ISS. ®
